content: The management system for morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) is based on community-driven home care. The stakeholders responsible for implementing and supervising MMDP activities include community-based care organizations such as health workers, women’s groups, and youth groups, whose involvement should be supervised. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) should also be coordinated and supervised. Additionally, individuals with or without expertise in community-based care can contribute to ensuring proper organization and coordination. Religious and community leaders, as well as traditional healers and members of faith-based organizations, are also key participants. Programs may establish teams of individuals interested in improving the health and well-being of patients with lymphatic filariasis (LF) in their communities. These teams could include representatives from local NGOs, community-based care organizations, or volunteers from women’s groups, support groups, self-help groups, youth groups, or corporate groups. Membership should broadly represent the community. Advocacy and social mobilization are essential to promote MMDP activities at various levels, ensuring smooth implementation and the involvement of all relevant actors. Advocacy efforts should target specific audiences, such as health sector decision-makers, donors, policymakers, community leaders, religious leaders, opinion leaders, and teachers. These efforts may include policy briefs, success stories, and targeted messages to increase knowledge, awareness, and support for prevention activities, budget allocation, and coordination. Program managers, doctors, nurses, and public health workers should collaborate in operations, monitoring, and evaluation. Research scientists and medical laboratories can contribute through forum discussions and research initiatives. Community health workers and volunteers should receive training to raise awareness and foster commitment. The general community, including young people and schoolchildren, should be educated through information, education, and communication materials to encourage behavioral change and awareness. Educating patients, their families, and schoolchildren about health is critical for managing morbidity and preventing disability. National programs may also conduct broader social mobilization campaigns depending on factors such as disease burden, hygiene practices, stigma levels, and available resources. Social mobilization can be integrated into mass drug administration campaigns or similar activities for other disabling diseases. It aims to inform the population about the disease and its consequences, modify attitudes (especially regarding stigma), and encourage early screening and active participation in case identification. Social mobilization can also promote improved hygiene practices to prevent acute episodes, particularly in individuals with subclinical lymphatic damage, and increase compliance with mass drug administration. Developing a social mobilization strategy requires specialized skills, and programs are encouraged to collaborate with experts in this field. Training should focus on competencies such as recognizing the disease and its complications, understanding home-based and long-term care, managing lymphedema and elephantiasis, and establishing appropriate follow-up, monitoring, and referral systems. Training materials may include modules for trainers and learners, flipcharts for health workers, and posters for patients. WHO has developed a training package to assist regions and countries in planning, implementing, and evaluating MMDP activities. Health care staff and caregivers should be trained to provide accurate information to patients with lymphedema or hydrocele about self-care, appropriate actions, and indications for hydrocelectomy. Training programs should include case management guidelines for identifying and managing acute attacks and lymphedema, tailored to the needs of health staff. Modules on morbidity and disability due to LF should also be integrated into medical and nursing school curricula. Psychological support and socioeconomic rehabilitation are essential to complement medical and surgical care for patients, helping them overcome stigma and shame and achieve full integration into their communities. Actions to prevent stigma include discussing the relevance of psychological support with health counselors, establishing referral systems for psychological services, and training health care staff and community health workers to screen for and provide psychological support. Support groups for individuals with LF can be created to share experiences and provide mutual support. Socioeconomic rehabilitation may involve organizing social mobilization campaigns to reduce stigma, discussing social inclusion and income-generating activities with welfare or finance services, and assessing the socioeconomic needs of individuals with LF. Preliminary social support can be provided by integrating individuals with LF into existing income-generating activities. At the district and community levels, health facilities can serve as technical referral centers, providing access to treatment for complicated cases, offering medical training and supervision to community health workers, and conducting monitoring and evaluation activities. Specific LF teams may be formed in areas with a high disease burden or many stakeholders. Community teams with diverse professional profiles can also be established to improve the status of LF patients in their communities. For example, district health workers can be trained by national-level trainers, who can then train community health workers. Community health workers can, in turn, train lymphedema patients and their families in their homes. For hydrocele management, national-level trainers can train regional and district-level physicians and surgeons. Implementation involves setting up follow-up systems and activities such as social mobilization, lymphedema management, hydrocele surgery, psychological support, and socioeconomic rehabilitation. The choice of delivery strategy for lymphedema management depends on the number and geographical distribution of cases. Hydrocelectomy should be made accessible to patients, with surgical services provided at the nearest available facility. Training programs for surgeons should cover diagnostic procedures, surgical techniques, infection control, and post-operative care. Monitoring and evaluation of MMDP programs are essential to track progress, assess impact, and prepare for the elimination of LF as a public health problem. Countries should document patient estimates, the availability of essential care packages, and the number of designated health facilities providing services for lymphedema and hydrocele.
